lesson.title: Measuring the Invisible: The Science of Calorimetry
lesson.summary: Calorimetry is the technique of measuring heat flow indirectly, by monitoring a temperature change and using conservation of energy to determine how much heat a chemical or physical process released or absorbed.
lesson.body:
You cannot see heat, weigh it, or watch it move directly. What you can measure is temperature, and because heat transfer and temperature change are linked through q = m c delta T, tracking temperature gives you an indirect but precise window into heat itself. Calorimetry is the general name for this strategy: place a process of interest, a chemical reaction or a physical change, inside a container called a calorimeter, monitor the temperature change of the known substance inside (almost always water, because its specific heat capacity is so well established), and use that temperature change to calculate exactly how much heat was released or absorbed.

The technique rests entirely on conservation of energy. If a calorimeter is well insulated so that no heat escapes to the outside lab, then whatever heat is lost by one part of the system must be gained by another part, with nothing left over. In equation form, q lost equals negative q gained, or more precisely, q(released by the process) = negative q(absorbed by the surroundings inside the calorimeter). This is the master equation of calorimetry, and virtually every calculation in this unit is some variation of setting one q term equal to the negative of another.

Not all calorimeters are alike, and the type of device changes exactly what quantity you end up measuring. A coffee cup calorimeter is open to the atmosphere and operates at constant pressure, which, as you will see in the next two chapters, means it measures enthalpy change directly. A bomb calorimeter is a sealed, rigid vessel that operates at constant volume, which means it measures a slightly different quantity, the internal energy change. Both designs rely on the exact same underlying principle of conservation of energy. They simply hold different variables fixed while the reaction happens inside them.

Here is a classic calorimetry problem: a 30.0 g sample of an unknown metal, initially at 95.0 degrees C, is dropped into 100.0 g of water initially at 22.0 degrees C, inside an insulated cup. The mixture is stirred and settles at a final temperature of 25.2 degrees C. Assuming no heat escapes to the surroundings, find the specific heat capacity of the metal. Start with the water, since its specific heat capacity is known: delta T(water) = 25.2 minus 22.0 = 3.2 degrees C, so q(water) = (100.0 g)(4.18 J/(g times degree C))(3.2 degrees C) = 1,337.6 J, meaning the water absorbed 1,337.6 J. By conservation of energy, the metal must have released exactly that much energy, so q(metal) = negative 1,337.6 J. The metal's own temperature change was delta T(metal) = 25.2 minus 95.0 = negative 69.8 degrees C. Solving q = m c delta T for c gives c = q divided by (m times delta T) = (negative 1,337.6 J) divided by (30.0 g times negative 69.8 degrees C) = negative 1,337.6 divided by negative 2,094 = 0.639 J/(g times degree C). Every calorimetry problem you meet is built from this same two step logic: find the heat gained (or lost) by the known substance, then set the unknown process equal to the opposite of that value. This idealization, that absolutely no heat escapes the calorimeter itself, is never perfectly true in a real experiment, which is exactly the kind of imperfection that specialized calorimeter designs try to minimize.
